procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated January 13, 1969 of the Division Bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, at Chandigarh, in L.F.A. No. 6 of 1969.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging certain orders. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition on November 6, 1968. The appellant then appealed to a Division Bench of the High Court, which dismissed the appeal in limine.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant was refused a certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court by the High Court. The appellant then asked for special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, which was granted on October 3, 1969.

decision.appeal_result: In the result this appeal succeeds.
directions: The judgment and order of the High Court are set aside.
The orders dated 27 February 1967 impugned in the appellant's petition before the High Court are quashed.
The appellant will get the costs of this appeal as well as the costs incurred below.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was denied a reasonable opportunity to reply to the show-cause notice, which led to his censure, on the grounds that the notice was too vague.

facts: The appellant received a show-cause notice proposing a penalty of censure.
The notice stated that the appellant's previous explanation, dated December 18, 1956, was considered "unsatisfactory."
The government argued that since the appellant knew the original charges and his own reply, simply being told his answer was "unsatisfactory" was sufficient.
The appellant contended that this notice was too vague to allow for an effective reply.
law: A show-cause notice must be precise and indicate the specific points on which the concerned officer is expected to reply.
The notice must provide a real and reasonable opportunity for the individual to defend themselves against the proposed action.
application: The Court found the show-cause notice to be "manifestly clear" and "too vague."
The notice failed to specify which part of the appellant's explanation was unsatisfactory, in what way it was unsatisfactory, or what materials the government relied on to reach that conclusion.
The Court noted that the notice did not even clarify whether it pertained to charge 1(a) or 1(b) of the original allegations.
By using only "vague general terms," the notice did not give the appellant any indication of the specific points he needed to address in his defense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the show-cause notice was too vague, which denied the appellant a real and reasonable opportunity to defend himself and show why he did not deserve the censure. Therefore, the Court accepted the appellant's contention.

issue.issue_text: Whether the order withholding pay in excess of the subsistence allowance for the period of suspension was liable to be struck down because it was passed without giving the appellant an opportunity to make a representation against it.

facts: After the appellant was reinstated, the government passed an order directing that for his period of suspension, he would not be paid anything more than the subsistence allowance he had already received.
This order was passed without giving the appellant an opportunity to make a representation against it.
law: The Court cited its previous judgment in *M. Gopala Krishna Naidu v. State of Madhya Pradesh*, which established that a government servant should be given an opportunity to be heard before a decision is made regarding their pay and allowances for a suspension period.
The Court also invoked the principles of justice and fair play, which demand that a person be given a reasonable opportunity to show cause before an order affecting their financial interests is made.
application: The Supreme Court found that the order withholding pay directly affected the appellant's pecuniary (financial) interest.

It rejected the High Court's view that this case was different from the *Naidu* case. The Supreme Court reasoned that because the government had withdrawn the disciplinary proceedings against the appellant, he never got the chance to prove that his suspension was unjustified.
Without the completion of the proceedings, the appellant had no opportunity to argue that he was entitled to his full pay and allowances for the suspension period.
Therefore, the Court determined that no real opportunity was given to the appellant to make an effective representation against the adverse order concerning his pay.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's contention, concluding that the order withholding his pay was liable to be struck down. The Court held that principles of justice and fair play required the government to give the appellant a reasonable opportunity to make a representation before passing an order that adversely affected his pay and emoluments.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was denied a reasonable opportunity to reply to the show-cause notice, which led to his censure, on the grounds that the notice was too vague.
appellant_arguments: The appellant did not get a reasonable opportunity to reply to the show-cause notice because it was too vague to enable him to give an effective reply.
respondent_arguments: Since the appellant was aware of the charge and his own reply, it was sufficient for the government to simply state that his answer was unsatisfactory.
Given that a lenient penalty of censure was being imposed, nothing more was required from the government in the notice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the order withholding pay in excess of the subsistence allowance for the period of suspension was liable to be struck down because it was passed without giving the appellant an opportunity to make a representation against it.
appellant_arguments: The order was liable to be struck down because it had been passed without giving the appellant any opportunity to make a representation against it.
respondent_arguments: Not mentioned in the provided text.

statutes.act_name: Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1952

cases.case_name: M. Gopala Krishan Naidu v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: An order under Fundamental Rule 54 is not always a consequential order. Since it can result in pecuniary loss to the government servant, the consideration is an objective function implying a duty to act judicially. An order passed without affording an opportunity to show cause is invalid for being in breach of the principles of natural justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a government authority makes an order that prejudicially affects a government servant's pay and emoluments, it is not a merely consequential administrative act but an objective function that implies a duty to act judicially; therefore, the principles of natural justice require that the employee be given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the proposed order.
obiter: Fundamental Rule 54(b) would be applicable in all cases where the officer concerned is not honourably acquitted.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the show-cause notice issued to the appellant was invalid because it was too vague to allow for a meaningful reply, and the subsequent order withholding his pay during suspension was also invalid because it was passed in violation of the principles of natural justice, as the appellant was not given an opportunity to be heard on a matter that caused him financial prejudice.
legal_tests_applied: A show-cause notice is invalid if it is too vague to enable the person to give an effective reply. Merely stating in general terms that a previous explanation was 'unsatisfactory' is insufficient.

If a government order affects an employee financially, it must be passed after an objective consideration of all relevant facts and circumstances, which implies a duty to act judicially and afford the affected person a full opportunity to make their case. An order passed without such an opportunity is invalid as it breaches the principles of natural justice.
policy_considerations: When an order may result in pecuniary loss to a Government servant, the consideration 'must be held to be an objective rather than a subjective function'.
The very nature of a function that can financially prejudice an employee 'implies the duty to act judicially.'

Principles of 'justice and fair play demand that the Government should have given the appellant a reasonable opportunity to show cause why an order affecting his pay and emoluments to his prejudice should not be made.'

An order passed without affording an opportunity to show cause in such circumstances is 'liable to be struck down as invalid on the ground that it is one in breach of the principles of natural justice'.
